claim: Octopus cells respond to multiple frequencies that change over time, as occurs in natural stimuli.
source: Unlike the average neuron, which integrates inputs over time on the order of tens of milliseconds, octopus cells must detect momentary coincidence of excitatory inputs from the cochlea during an ongoing sound on both the millisecond and submillisecond time scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of octopus cells.

claim: Octopus cells receive inhibitory inputs on their dendrites that enhance opportunities for coincidence detection in the cell body.
source: Here, we show that octopus cells receive inhibitory inputs on their dendrites that enhance opportunities for coincidence detection in the cell body, thereby allowing for responses both to rapid onsets at the beginning of a sound and to frequency modulations during the sound.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dendritic inhibition allows octopus cells to respond both to rapid onsets at the beginning of a sound and to frequency modulations during the sound.
source: Here, we show that octopus cells receive inhibitory inputs on their dendrites that enhance opportunities for coincidence detection in the cell body, thereby allowing for responses both to rapid onsets at the beginning of a sound and to frequency modulations during the sound.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by modeling and experimental data.

claim: Overlapping sounds are distinguished perceptually by correctly binding frequencies with coherent onsets and synchronized temporal modulations.
source: For instance, overlapping sounds, such as two competing speakers in a noisy room, are distinguished perceptually by correctly binding frequencies with coherent onsets and synchronized temporal modulations (Shamma et al., 2011; Pressnitzer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spiral ganglion neurons project through the eighth nerve, bifurcate, and spread tonotopically to fill each division of the cochlear nucleus complex.
source: Frequency information is communicated by spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), whose central axons, also called auditory nerve fibers, project through the eighth nerve, bifurcate, and spread tonotopically to fill each division of the cochlear nucleus complex (CNC; De No, 1933; Fekete et al., 1984; Liberman, 1991; Brown and Ledwith, 1990; Leake and Snyder, 1989; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: SGNs fall into physiologically distinct subtypes that are recruited at different intensities, allowing sounds to be detected across a wide dynamic range.
source: In addition, SGNs fall into physiologically distinct subtypes that are recruited at different intensities, allowing sounds to be detected across a wide dynamic range (Sachs and Abbas, 1974; Liberman, 1982; Liberman, 1978; Evans and Palmer, 1980; Taberner and Liberman, 2005; Palmer and Evans, 1980; Winter et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Octopus cells have low input resistances near rest (~4 MΩ).
source: Biophysically, octopus cells have low input resistances near rest (~4 MΩ; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000), fast time constants (~200 µs; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000; Bal and Oertel, 2001), and large low‐voltage‐activated potassium (~40 nS at rest; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2001), and hyperpolarization activated (~62 nS at rest; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000) conductances.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Octopus cells have fast time constants (~200 µs).
source: Biophysically, octopus cells have low input resistances near rest (~4 MΩ; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000), fast time constants (~200 µs; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000; Bal and Oertel, 2001), and large low‐voltage‐activated potassium (~40 nS at rest; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2001), and hyperpolarization activated (~62 nS at rest; Golding et al., 1999; Bal and Oertel, 2000) conductances.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Octopus cells have narrow windows of coincidence detection on the order of 1 ms.
source: Together these properties give octopus cells impressively narrow windows of coincidence detection on the order of 1 ms (Cao and Oertel, 2017; Golding et al., 1995; Golding and Oertel, 2012; Manis and Marx, 1991; Oertel, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Octopus cells can phase lock to broadband transients at rates up to 1 kHz.
source: Fittingly, in vivo recordings from octopus cells demonstrate their ability to phase lock to broadband transients at rates up to 1 kHz (Lu et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2005; Smith et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claim: The octopus cell area is not devoid of inhibitory inputs, although they are less prominent than in the surrounding CNC.
source: The teardrop-shaped OCA is not devoid of inhibitory inputs, although they are less prominent than in the surrounding CNC.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1B legend and shown in the image.

claim: The density of SGN inputs on octopus cell dendrites is higher (10.7 ± 3.0 SGN puncta/100 µm2) than that of inhibitory inputs (4.2 ± 0.8 puncta/100 µm2).
source: Consistent with qualitative assessment, the density of SGN inputs was higher (10.7 ± 3.0 SGN puncta/100 µm2) than that of inhibitory inputs (4.2 ± 0.8 puncta/100 µm2, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from reconstructions shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Octopus cells have a strikingly different average ratio of excitatory and inhibitory puncta on the soma (7:1) and on the dendrite (5:2).
source: As a result, octopus cells have a strikingly different average ratio of excitatory and inhibitory puncta on the soma (7:1) and on the dendrite (5:2), suggesting that each compartment contributes differentially to the final computation made by the octopus cell (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is calculated from the data and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There are three molecularly distinct SGN subtypes, referred to as Ia, Ib, and Ic SGNs, which correlate with previously shown physiological groups.
source: There are three molecularly distinct SGN subtypes, referred to as Ia, Ib, and Ic SGNs, which correlate with previously shown physiological groups (Liberman, 1978; Liberman et al., 2011; Liberman, 1982; Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Siebald et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2018; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Ntng1Cre-labeled Ib/c SGNs accounted for 60.1 ± 2.6% of the entire SGN population, with 28.5 ± 12.2% Ib SGNs, 31.6% Ic SGNs, and 39.9 ± 2.6% Ia SGNs.
source: As determined using the Ai14 tdTomato (tdT) reporter, Ntng1Cre-labeled Ib/c SGNs accounted for 60.1 ± 2.6% of the entire population, with 28.5 ± 12.2% Ib SGNs, 31.6% Ic SGNs, and 39.9 ± 2.6% Ia SGNs (Figure 2C: n=1599 neurons, 4 mice; mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cell counting shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Octopus cell dendrites received 4.1 ± 1.0 puncta/100 µm2 from Ib/c SGNs, accounting for 38% of the total SGN density.
source: Octopus cell dendrites received 4.1 ± 1.0 puncta/100 µm2 from Ib/c SGNs (Figure 2E, magenta: n=9 cells, 5 mice; mean ± SD), accounting for 38% of the total SGN density.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from reconstructions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ia SGNs accounted for 62 ± 9.7% of SGN synapses on octopus cells.
source: By contrast, Ia SGNs, which comprise ~40% of the total population (Figure 2C, yellow), accounted for 62 ± 9.7% of SGN synapses on octopus cells (Figure 2E, yellow: 6.6 ± 1.0 puncta/100 µm2).
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The average octopus cell receives ~1035 SGN synapses (642 Ia SGN, 393 Ib/c SGN) and ~354 inhibitory synapses.
source: Together, excitatory and inhibitory puncta densities in the innervation maps indicate the average octopus cell receives ~1035 SGN synapses (642 Ia SGN, 393 Ib/c SGN) and ~354 inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is calculated from the density measurements.

claim: 83% of the synapses were on the dendrites, suggesting a critical role in the octopus cell computation.
source: Additionally, 83% of the synapses were on the dendrites, suggesting a critical role in the octopus cell computation.
evidence: This is calculated from the data and includes an inference about functional significance.

claim: Trains of ChR2-evoked EPSPs in both the total SGN population and the Ib/c SGN population exhibited no differences in paired-pulse plasticity at any frequency of stimulation.
source: Trains of ChR2-evoked EPSPs, ranging from 5 to 50 Hz, in both the total SGN population (Figure 3B, black: n=8 cells, 5 mice) and the Ib/c SGN population (Figure 3B, magenta: n=7 cells, 6 mice) exhibited no differences in paired-pulse plasticity at any frequency of stimulation (p>0.35 at all interstimulus intervals, Tukey's HSD), although the Ib/c population exhibited higher variability than the total SGN population (at 20ms: total SGN SD=0.11, Ib/c SGN SD=0.24).
evidence: This is a statistical result from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Electrically-evoked EPSPs had higher paired-pulse ratios than ChR2-evoked EPSPs and were mildly facilitating at short (20 ms) intervals.
source: Electrically-evoked EPSPs had higher paired-pulse ratios than ChR2-evoked EPSPs and were mildly facilitating at short (20 ms) intervals (Figure 3B–C, open circles: n=5 cells, 3 mice), consistent with an octopus cell's ability to respond reliably to click trains in vivo (Godfrey et al., 1975; Rhode et al., 1983; Smith et al., 2005; Oertel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3B-C and compared to previous in vivo studies.

claim: ChR2-evoked synaptic responses undergo synaptic depression.
source: ChR2-evoked synaptic responses are known to undergo synaptic depression (Jackman et al., 2014; Zhang and Oertner, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Electrically evoked EPSPs with non-physiological calcium concentrations (2.4 mM) resulted in short-term depression at 50 Hz of electrical stimulation.
source: We repeated paired-pulse plasticity experiments with non-physiological calcium concentrations (2.4 mM) and similarly found that electrically evoked EPSPs from SGNs resulted in short-term depression at 50 Hz of electrical stimulation (Figure 3C, grey: n=3 cells, 2 mice), although not to the degree observed when using full-field, ChR2-evoked inputs (Figure 3C, black: n=8 cells, 5 mice).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Light-evoked (Slc6a5-ChR2) inhibitory post synaptic potentials (IPSPs) were not observed in octopus cell somas during whole-cell current clamp recordings from P30-45 mice under control conditions.
source: Similarly, we did not observe light-evoked (Slc6a5-ChR2) inhibitory post synaptic potentials (IPSPs) in octopus cell somas during whole-cell current clamp recordings from P30-45 mice.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Pharmacologically reducing conductances from voltage-gated potassium (Kv) and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels increased octopus cell membrane resistance and hyperpolarized the resting membrane potential by ~8–10 mV.
source: This cocktail increased octopus cell membrane resistance and hyperpolarized the resting membrane potential by ~8–10 mV (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The increase in input resistance unveiled light-evoked IPSPs in recordings from octopus cell somas.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the increase in input resistance unveiled light-evoked IPSPs in recordings from octopus cell somas (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Light-evoked IPSPs were fully abolished by bath application of 500 nM strychnine (STN), confirming the presence of functional glycinergic inhibitory synaptic transmission onto octopus cells.
source: Additionally, these IPSPs were fully abolished by bath application of 500 nM strychnine (STN) (Figure 4C), confirming the presence of functional glycinergic inhibitory synaptic transmission onto octopus cells.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Relevant glycine receptors include both large conductance extrasynaptic β-subunit lacking homomeric receptors and synaptically localized α2β receptors with slower kinetics.
source: These results indicate that relevant glycine receptors include both large conductance extrasynaptic β-subunit lacking homomeric receptors and synaptically localized α2β receptors with slower kinetics (Lynch, 2009; Veruki et al., 2007; Dutertre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from pharmacological experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Removal of Kv and HCN conductances in the model changed the input resistance and current-voltage relationship of the neuron, resulting in reduced electrotonic isolation.
source: As in our current-clamp recordings (Figure 4A), removal of Kv and HCN conductances in the model changed the input resistance and current-voltage relationship of the neuron, resulting in reduced electrotonic isolation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Activation of large (10nS) dendritic glycinergic conductances induced negligible hyperpolarizing voltage changes in the model.
source: Activation of large (10nS) dendritic glycinergic conductances induced negligible hyperpolarizing voltage changes in the model (Figure 4F, black).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4F.

claim: With increased input resistance and reduced electrotonic isolation after Kv and HCN block, dendritic IPSPs measured at the soma were detectable.
source: With increased input resistance and reduced electrotonic isolation after Kv and HCN block, dendritic IPSPs measured at the soma were detectable (Figure 4F, blue), consistent with our in vitro recordings.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4F that matches experimental data.

claim: Kv and HCN block increased the magnitude of soma-measured IPSPs for all glycine conductances.
source: Kv and HCN block and the resulting change in input resistance increased the magnitude of soma-measured IPSPs for all glycine conductances (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Following the pharmacological blockade of Kv and HCN channels, there was either a reduction in the amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at distal synapses or little change in IPSC amplitude at proximal synapses.
source: In contrast, following the pharmacological blockade of Kv and HCN channels, we observed either a reduction in the amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at distal synapses (Figure 4H, blue) or little change in IPSC amplitude at proximal synapses (Figure 4H, orange).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Alterations in IPSCs are unlikely to account for the observed increase in inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) magnitude recorded at the soma after Kv and HCN channel block.
source: These findings indicate that alterations in IPSCs are unlikely to account for the observed increase in inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) magnitude recorded at the soma after Kv and HCN channel block (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: Transfer impedance (ZT), a measure of signal transmission efficiency, was dramatically increased after Kv and HCN block.
source: Transfer impedance (ZT), a measure of signal transmission efficiency, was dramatically increased after Kv and HCN block (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Inhibitory synapses that are located proximally to excitation had less of an influence on excitation recorded at the soma compared to those inhibitory synapses located distally to excitation.
source: In our model, inhibitory synapses that are located proximally to excitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) had less of an influence on excitation recorded at the soma compared to those inhibitory synapses located distally to excitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model predicted that inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude and accelerates EPSP peak timing at the soma for both inhibition proximal to excitation and inhibition distal to excitation.
source: For both inhibition proximal to excitation (Figure 5B–C) and inhibition distal to excitation (Figure 5D–E), the model predicted that inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude and accelerates EPSP peak timing at the soma.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: When synaptic inhibition was evoked together with excitation, EPSPs recorded in the soma were smaller and faster than when excitation was evoked alone.
source: When synaptic inhibition was evoked together with excitation (Figure 5F, green), EPSPs recorded in the soma were smaller and faster than when excitation was evoked alone (Figure 5F, black: n=8 cells, 6 mice).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ChR2-evoked inhibition decreased EPSP heights by 25.2 ± 9.0% and shifted the peak of EPSPs forward 57.5 ± 26 µs.
source: ChR2-evoked inhibition decreased EPSP heights by 25.2 ± 9.0% (Figure 5G, green) and shifted the peak of EPSPs forward 57.5 ± 26 µs (Figure 5H, green).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Bath application of 25 µM glycine mimicked the effect of ChR2-evoked inhibition on EPSPs.
source: This effect was mimicked by bath application of 25 µM glycine (Figure 5G–H, blue: n=4 cells, 3 mice).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Bath application of 1 µM STN resulted in larger EPSPs and delayed peak times.
source: Further, bath application of 1 µM STN had the opposite effect, resulting in larger EPSPs and delayed peak times (Figure 5F–H, orange: n=5 cells, 4 mice).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The timing of EPSP arrival in the soma may be shaped both by tonically active glycine channels and the release of synaptic glycine onto the dendrite.
source: These findings suggest that the timing of EPSP arrival in the soma may be shaped both by tonically active glycine channels and the release of synaptic glycine onto the dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with glycine and strychnine.

claim: Many SGNs terminate on the octopus cell soma, where inhibition is minimal.
source: Of note, many SGNs also terminate on the octopus cell soma, where inhibition is minimal.
evidence: This is based on the anatomical data showing high excitatory and low inhibitory puncta density on the soma.

claim: The octopus cell's ability to act as a coincidence detector depends on two stages of compartmentalized computations, one in the dendrite that combines excitation and inhibition and one in the soma that is restricted by the rigid temporal summation window for coincidence detection.
source: This suggests that the octopus cell's ability to act as a coincidence detector depends on two stages of compartmentalized computations, one in the dendrite that combines excitation and inhibition to provide important information about which frequencies co-occur in a complex sound stimulus and one in the soma that is restricted by the rigid temporal summation window for coincidence detection.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Octopus cells respond well to cues that include complex spectrotemporal patterns, including frequency modulations beyond the onset of the stimulus.
source: As shown by in vivo recordings (Recio-Spinoso and Rhode, 2020; Lu et al., 2022), octopus cells respond well to cues that include complex spectrotemporal patterns, including frequency modulations beyond the onset of the stimulus (Lu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claim: The addition of dendritic inhibition transforms the magnitude and timing of SGN signals as they arrive in the cell body, which may expand the response selectivity of an octopus cell.
source: The results suggest that, in addition to high Kv and HCN conductances at rest, the addition of dendritic inhibition transforms the magnitude and timing of SGN signals as they arrive in the cell body, which may expand the response selectivity of an octopus cell and allow them to become a slightly leakier integrator that can accumulate evidence beyond onsets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The majority of inputs onto octopus cells come from Ia SGNs, which most closely correspond to the low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate population.
source: We find that the majority of inputs onto octopus cells come from Ia SGNs, which most closely correspond to the low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate population.
evidence: This is based on the quantitative anatomical data showing Ia SGN dominance.

claim: Single-unit SGN recordings in cats demonstrated a bias towards low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate axon collaterals in the octopus cell area.
source: Consistent with this result, single-unit SGN recordings in cats demonstrated a bias towards low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate axon collaterals in the octopus cell area (Liberman, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work in cats.

claim: Low-threshold SGNs are characterized by short first spike latencies and low temporal jitter.
source: Low-threshold SGNs are also characterized by short first spike latencies and low temporal jitter (Buran et al., 2010; Oliver et al., 2006; Bourien et al., 2014; Costalupes et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The presence of many low-threshold and temporally precise inputs on the octopus cell may help ensure that coincidence detection still works reliably for quiet sounds.
source: The presence of many low-threshold and temporally precise inputs on the octopus cell may help ensure that coincidence detection still works reliably for quiet sounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of Ia SGNs and their dominance on octopus cells.

claim: Ia inputs onto octopus cells do not exhibit paired-pulse depression, similar to low levels of depression seen in Ia inputs to bushy cells.
source: Further, Ia inputs onto octopus cells do not exhibit paired-pulse depression, similar to low levels of depression seen in Ia inputs to bushy cells (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and supported by a citation to work on bushy cells.

claim: Recruitment of higher threshold SGNs at higher sound intensities may compensate for saturation of precise, low-threshold SGN responses by background noise.
source: Since precise, low-threshold SGN responses can be saturated by background noise such that responses to relevant stimuli are masked (Liberman, 1978; Costalupes et al., 1984; Bourien et al., 2014; Huet et al., 2016), recruitment of higher threshold SGNs at higher sound intensities may compensate for this tradeoff.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of different SGN subtypes and supported by citations.

claim: Resting conductances and low-threshold potassium conductances may suppress voltage-gated calcium spikes and attenuate the magnitude of action potentials as they backpropagate through the soma and dendritic tree in octopus cells.
source: Resting conductances and low-threshold potassium conductances may suppress voltage-gated calcium spikes and attenuate the magnitude of action potentials as they backpropagate through the soma and dendritic tree (Golding et al., 1999; Cao and Oertel, 2005; Bal and Baydas, 2009; Bal and Oertel, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Subthreshold dendritic integration of coincident excitation and local inhibition may be the primary computation that occurs in octopus cell dendrites before action potential generation near the soma.
source: Therefore, subthreshold dendritic integration of coincident excitation and local inhibition may be the primary computation that occurs in octopus cell dendrites before action potential generation near the soma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical properties of octopus cells.

claim: It is unknown where glycinergic innervation to octopus cells originates.
source: Although this work uncovers a role for inhibition, a deeper understanding of octopus cell computations will require determining what information is carried by inhibitory inputs. Despite the well-established presence of presynaptic glycinergic puncta in the octopus cell area (Kemmer and Vater, 1997; Kolston et al., 1992; Juiz et al., 1996; Moore et al., 1996) and glycinergic receptor expression in octopus cells (Friauf et al., 1997; Sato et al., 2000; Schofield and Cant, 1996; Thompson et al., 1985; Adams and Mugnaini, 1987), it is unknown where glycinergic innervation originates.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge despite previous anatomical studies.

claim: It remains unclear whether octopus cells receive connections from D-Stellate, L-Stellate, or tuberculoventral cells.
source: Local neurons within the CNC could provide inhibition; however it remains unclear whether octopus cells receive connections from D-Stellate (Oertel et al., 1990), L-Stellate (Ngodup et al., 2020), or tuberculoventral cells (Wickesberg et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as uncertain and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Terminal degeneration experiments in cats suggested the superior periolivary nucleus (SPON) and the ventral division of the lateral lemniscus (VNLL) as potential sources of descending inhibition to the octopus cell area.
source: Outside of the CNC, terminal degeneration experiments in cats suggested the superior periolivary nucleus (SPON) and the ventral division of the lateral lemniscus (VNLL) as potential sources of descending inhibition to the octopus cell area (Kane, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work in cats.

claim: Octopus cells provide excitatory input to both the SPON and the VNLL.
source: Octopus cells provide excitatory input to both the SPON (Friauf and Ostwald, 1988; Schofield, 1995; Thompson and Thompson, 1991; Zook and Casseday, 1985; Felix Ii et al., 2017) and the VNLL (Schofield and Cant, 1997; Smith et al., 2005; Berger et al., 2014; Nayagam et al., 2005; Adams, 1997; Vater and Feng, 1990), raising the possibility of feedback inhibition from the auditory brainstem as a circuit mechanism that elongates temporal summation windows during ongoing stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Descending feedback inhibition is not rapid enough to prevent or alter the characteristic octopus cell onset response, but could change the effective coincidence detection window as the stimulus continues or limit the duration of the response.
source: Such descending feedback inhibition is not rapid enough to prevent or alter the characteristic octopus cell onset response, but could change the effective coincidence detection window as the stimulus continues or limit the duration of the response.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential role of feedback inhibition.
